title: On-Call & Incident Response
summary: The operational process and roles for handling an active incident, and the blameless postmortem that turns it into a lasting fix.

slides.markdown:
**On-call** is the rotation of engineers responsible for responding when something breaks; **incident response** is the structured process they follow once paged.

- Roles and severities exist so a crisis doesn't also require inventing a process on the spot.
- An **incident commander** coordinates — they don't necessarily fix anything themselves.
- Every real incident ends in a **blameless postmortem** — the mechanism that turns pain into prevention.

slides.subTitle: Primary, secondary, follow-the-sun
slides.markdown:
A rotation typically has a **primary** on-call (first paged) and a **secondary** (backup, paged on escalation or no-ack). Rotations are usually weekly, sized so no one is on-call constantly enough to burn out.

Globally distributed teams often run **follow-the-sun**: on-call responsibility hands off to whichever region is in business hours, avoiding 3am pages entirely for teams with true 24/7 coverage. Escalation paths define exactly who gets paged next, and after how long, if the current responder doesn't acknowledge.

slides.subTitle: What SEV1 vs SEV2 actually changes
slides.markdown:
| | SEV1 | SEV2 | SEV3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impact | Full outage / data loss risk | Partial degradation, major feature down | Minor, workaround exists |
| Response | All-hands, IC assigned immediately | On-call + relevant team, IC often assigned | Ticket, normal business hours |
| Comms | Status page, exec updates | Internal updates, maybe status page | Internal only |

Severity isn't just a label — it changes **who gets paged, how fast, and who gets told**, which is exactly why misjudging it (over- or under-declaring) causes real damage either way.

slides.subTitle: Coordinating without fixing
slides.markdown:
The **Incident Commander (IC)** owns the *process* of the incident, not the technical fix. Their job: keep track of who's doing what, make the call on severity and comms, decide when to escalate or bring in more people, and — critically — **not** get pulled into debugging themselves.

This separation matters because the person best qualified to fix the bug is rarely also well-positioned to track five parallel workstreams and manage stakeholder updates at the same time. Splitting the roles keeps both moving.

Communication is a **first-class incident task**, not an afterthought squeezed in between fixes. It runs on three channels simultaneously: a **status page** for customers, an **internal channel** for responders to coordinate in real time, and periodic **stakeholder updates** for leadership who need the summary, not the debugging noise.

A good comms cadence — e.g. an update every 30 minutes even if the update is "still investigating" — prevents the worst failure mode: silence, which reads as either incompetence or a cover-up even when the team is working hard.

slides.subTitle: Page to resolution to postmortem
slides.markdown:
![An incident's timeline from page to resolution to postmortem](assets/incident-timeline.svg)

Every stage produces artifacts that feed the postmortem later: when the alert fired, when it was acknowledged, what mitigated it, and when it was confirmed resolved. Capturing timestamps in real time beats reconstructing them afterward from memory.

slides.subTitle: Why "blameless" is a mechanism, not a nicety
slides.markdown:
A **blameless postmortem** treats the incident as a symptom of the system's design, process, and tooling — not a person's mistake. This isn't just kindness: it's what makes people **tell the truth**. If admitting "I ran the wrong command" gets you blamed, the next engineer in that position quietly works around the postmortem instead of surfacing the real chain of events.

Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free — it means the analysis stays focused on "what let this happen" (a missing safeguard, a confusing runbook) rather than "who do we discipline."

A useful postmortem has four sections that don't get skipped: a **timeline** (what happened, when, in order), the **impact** (users affected, duration, error budget spent), the **root cause(s)** (plural — most incidents have several contributing factors, not one), and **action items** with owners and due dates.

The action items are the entire point — a postmortem that's well-written but produces no tracked follow-up is a story, not a fix.

slides.subTitle: An action item that actually prevents recurrence
slides.markdown:
| Action item | Does it prevent recurrence? |
|---|---|
| "Be more careful when deploying config changes" | No — relies on human vigilance, not a system change |
| "Add a pre-deploy validation check that rejects configs missing a required field" | Yes — a structural safeguard that catches the same mistake automatically next time |

The difference is whether the fix survives the next tired engineer at 2am. "Be more careful" fails; a validation gate, a required approval, or a type check succeeds because it doesn't depend on anyone remembering.
